modern_related_concept: Metabolic disorders involving excess urination / polyuria
traditional_description: Prameha is a group of disorders described in Ayurvedic classical texts (Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita) characterized by excess and turbid urination. The texts describe 20 types of Prameha based on Dosha predominance (Vataja, Pittaja, Kaphaja) and the nature of the urine. Prameha is considered a Santarpanaja vyadhi (disease of over-nourishment) and is associated with sedentary lifestyle, excessive intake of heavy, sweet, and fatty foods.
classical_context: Described in Charaka Samhita, Nidana Sthana; Sushruta Samhita, Nidana Sthana. Included among the Ashtamahagada (eight great diseases).
modern_evidence_status: Partly overlapping concept. Prameha as a category overlaps with but is not identical to modern diabetes mellitus. Some research has explored Ayurvedic anti-Prameha herbs (e.g., Gymnema sylvestre, Bitter melon) for blood sugar effects; evidence varies in quality. The two frameworks use different diagnostic concepts and should not be automatically equated.
safety_considerations: Do not use Ayurvedic interventions to replace prescribed diabetes medication without medical supervision. Some herbs can interact with antidiabetic drugs.

modern_related_concept: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (conceptual analogue — not identical)
traditional_description: Madhumeha is the most severe and incurable (Asadhya) form of Prameha described in Ayurvedic texts. The term means 'honey urine' — referring to the sweet, pale, and abundant nature of the urine. Classical texts describe it as predominantly Vataja (Vata-predominant) in origin. Patients are described as thin, weak, with intense thirst and wasting — which may correspond to what we now recognize as Type 1 or insulin-deficient presentations, though the mapping is not exact.
classical_context: Charaka Samhita describes Madhumeha under Vataja Prameha. Sushruta considers it both inherited (Sahaja Prameha, analogous to type 1) and acquired (Apathyanimittaja Prameha, analogous to type 2).
modern_evidence_status: Partly overlapping. Madhumeha is frequently discussed as an Ayurvedic analogue of diabetes mellitus. However, the diagnostic criteria, pathophysiology, and classifications differ significantly. Research on Ayurvedic anti-Prameha treatments (e.g., Vijayasar, Gudmar, Karela) shows variable evidence quality. None replace modern antidiabetic therapy.
relationship: Traditional analogue — partly overlapping — important conceptual distinctions exist
safety_considerations: Madhumeha treatment in Ayurveda involves complex multi-modal protocols. Patients on insulin or oral antidiabetics must not change or stop medication based on Ayurvedic consultation without their treating physician's involvement.

traditional_description: Jwara is described as one of the most important diseases in Ayurveda and is given prominent coverage in classical texts. It is characterized by abnormal heat sensation, body ache, loss of appetite, and general malaise. Classical texts describe 8 types of Jwara based on Dosha predominance and etiology. Nija Jwara (intrinsic fever) and Agantuka Jwara (exogenous fever, including infectious fever) are key classifications.
classical_context: Jwara is treated first among diseases in Charaka Samhita's Chikitsa Sthana (Chapter 3) because it is considered the 'king of diseases' (Jwaranam Raja). Described in all major classical Ayurvedic texts.
modern_evidence_status: Partly overlapping. Modern fever is a non-specific response to infection, inflammation, or other causes. Ayurvedic Jwara encompasses similar symptomatology but from a different etiological framework. Some Ayurvedic herbs used in Jwara management (e.g., Tulsi / Ocimum sanctum, Guduchi / Tinospora cordifolia) have been studied for antipyretic and immunomodulatory properties — evidence is preliminary.
relationship: Partly overlapping — similar symptoms, different conceptual framework
safety_considerations: High fever, especially in children, requires prompt modern medical evaluation. Ayurvedic home remedies may complement care for mild symptoms but do not replace medical evaluation for persistent or high-grade fever.

traditional_description: Shwasa refers to a group of conditions characterized by difficult, labored, or abnormal breathing. Classical Ayurvedic texts describe five types: Mahashwasa, Urdhvashwasa, Chinashwasa, Tamaka Shwasa, and Ksudra Shwasa. Tamaka Shwasa is the most clinically relevant and has been historically compared to bronchial asthma — characterized by paroxysmal episodes, nocturnal worsening, relief in sitting position, and associated with Kapha and Vata imbalance.
classical_context: Described in Charaka Samhita — Chikitsa Sthana, Chapter 17; Sushruta Samhita; Ashtanga Hridayam — Nidana and Chikitsa Sthana.
modern_evidence_status: Partly overlapping. Tamaka Shwasa has been widely studied as an analogue of bronchial asthma. Some Ayurvedic formulations (e.g., Vasa / Adhatoda vasica, Pushkarmool / Inula racemosa, Sitopaladi churna) have been studied for bronchodilatory or anti-inflammatory effects. Evidence quality is variable and more rigorous trials are needed.
relationship: Partly overlapping / traditional analogue (especially Tamaka Shwasa ≈ bronchial asthma)
safety_considerations: Asthma and other respiratory conditions require modern medical management. Ayurvedic approaches may complement but must not replace prescribed inhalers or corticosteroids.

traditional_description: Ahara (food/diet) is considered the most fundamental pillar of health in Ayurveda. The texts elaborate on the concept of Pathya (wholesome, appropriate food) and Apathya (unwholesome, inappropriate food) for each condition. Ahara is classified by its Rasa (taste — 6 types: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, astringent), Guna (qualities), Vipaka (post-digestive effect), and Prabhava (specific action). The concept of Agni (digestive fire) is central — poor Agni leads to formation of Ama (undigested metabolic waste), considered the root of disease.
classical_context: Charaka Samhita — Sutra Sthana, Chapter 27 (Annapanavidhi Adhyaya) and Chapter 25 (Yajjah Purushiya Adhyaya); Ashtanga Hridayam — Sutra Sthana.
modern_evidence_status: Partially validated. Some specific Ayurvedic dietary recommendations align with modern nutritional science (e.g., fiber-rich diet for metabolic health, avoiding processed sugar). The underlying conceptual framework (Dosha, Agni, Ama) does not have direct equivalents in modern nutritional science.
relationship: Partly overlapping — different conceptual frameworks, some practical overlap
safety_considerations: Extreme dietary restrictions without medical supervision can be harmful. Consult a registered dietitian for personalized dietary advice.

traditional_description: Vihara encompasses all behavioral and lifestyle practices that maintain or restore health in Ayurveda. This includes Dinacharya (daily routine), Ritucharya (seasonal routine), exercise (Vyayama), sleep (Nidra), and behavioral ethics (Sadvritta). Proper sleep, seasonal adaptation of diet and lifestyle, regulated exercise, and mental discipline are considered essential for maintaining Dosha balance.
classical_context: Charaka Samhita — Sutra Sthana, Chapters 5-7; Ashtanga Hridayam — Sutra Sthana, Chapters 2-4.
modern_evidence_status: Several Vihara principles align with evidence-based lifestyle medicine (regular sleep, exercise, stress management). Research on concepts like Dinacharya has explored circadian biology connections. The broader Dosha framework does not have direct modern equivalents.
relationship: Partly overlapping — lifestyle principles have conceptual parallels
safety_considerations: Extreme fasting, purification procedures (Panchakarma), or vigorous exercise without professional guidance can be harmful.

traditional_description: Guduchi (also called Amrita or Giloy) is one of the most important herbs in Ayurvedic medicine. It is classified as a Rasayana (rejuvenating herb) and is described as Tridoshahara (balancing all three Doshas). Classical texts attribute properties including antipyretic, anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, anti-diabetic, and hepatoprotective effects. It is commonly used in Jwara (fever), Prameha, and general debility.
classical_context: Charaka Samhita — Sutra Sthana, described among Medhya Rasayanas (brain tonics) and Jwarahara dravyas. Ashtanga Hridayam — extensively described.
modern_evidence_status: Limited to moderate evidence. Several animal studies and small human trials suggest immunomodulatory, antipyretic, and anti-hyperglycemic properties. The active constituents (tinosporine, berberine, columbin, tinosporide) have been studied. However, large randomized controlled trials are limited. Some reports of cholestatic hepatitis associated with Guduchi products, particularly during COVID-19 treatment attempts.
relationship: Traditional herb — preliminary modern evidence — quality RCTs limited
safety_considerations: Generally considered safe at traditional doses. However, liver injury has been reported. Avoid in autoimmune conditions or immunosuppressed patients. Verify product quality. Do not use to replace prescribed treatments.

traditional_description: Ashwagandha is one of the most important Rasayana herbs in Ayurveda. The name means 'smell of horse' — referring to the root's distinctive odor and the traditional belief that it imparts the strength of a horse. It is classified as a Balya (strength-promoting), Shukrala (reproductive tonic), Medhya (cognition-enhancing), and general Rasayana. Used for debility, emaciation, stress-related conditions, and as a general health tonic.
classical_context: Charaka Samhita — Chikitsa Sthana, Chapter 1 (Rasayana Adhyaya); Ashtanga Hridayam — Uttara Sthana; extensively described in Dhanvantari Nighantu.
modern_evidence_status: Moderate evidence for some effects. Multiple human clinical trials have studied Ashwagandha for stress and anxiety reduction, athletic performance, thyroid function (TSH reduction), male fertility, and cognitive function. Cochrane-quality reviews are limited. Several randomized controlled trials support adaptogenic effects. Active constituents: withanolides. Generally regarded as safe at studied doses. Some thyroid-stimulating effects reported — caution in hyperthyroidism.
relationship: Traditional herb — moderate modern evidence for adaptogenic effects
safety_considerations: Generally well-tolerated at recommended doses. Rare: liver injury reported. Avoid in pregnancy (uterine stimulating potential). Caution in hyperthyroidism, thyroid medications, and immunosuppressants. Use standardized extracts.
sources: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

traditional_description: Triphala is one of the most widely used classical Ayurvedic formulations, consisting of three fruits: Amalaki (Phyllanthus emblica / Indian gooseberry), Bibhitaki (Terminalia bellirica), and Haritaki (Terminalia chebula). It is described as a Tridoshahara (balancing all three Doshas) formulation and is used for digestive health, as a mild laxative, as a Rasayana, and for eye health. The texts describe it as suitable for long-term use.
classical_context: Described in Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, and Ashtanga Hridayam. One of the most frequently prescribed formulations in classical Ayurveda.
modern_evidence_status: Limited to moderate evidence. Research has explored antioxidant properties (especially Amalaki's high vitamin C content), prebiotic effects on gut microbiome, anti-inflammatory effects, and mild laxative properties. Some preliminary evidence for metabolic effects. Quality RCTs are limited.
safety_considerations: Generally regarded as safe at recommended doses. High doses may cause loose stools. May interact with diabetes medications (some evidence of blood glucose effects). Do not use in acute diarrhea or dehydration. Consult healthcare provider before using with prescription medications.
sources: Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine

modern_related_concept: Conceptual framework for constitution and disease classification
traditional_description: The Tridosha theory is the fundamental conceptual framework of Ayurveda. It posits that all physiological and pathological processes in the body are governed by three dynamic principles (Doshas): Vata (related to movement, nervous system, breath), Pitta (related to transformation, metabolism, digestion), and Kapha (related to structure, lubrication, immunity). Health is defined as the balanced state of all three Doshas; disease arises from imbalance. Each individual has a unique constitutional Dosha pattern (Prakriti).
classical_context: The Tridosha theory is foundational to all classical Ayurvedic texts — Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, Ashtanga Hridayam. It forms the basis for diagnosis (Rogi and Roga Pariksha), treatment selection, and dietary/lifestyle recommendations.
modern_evidence_status: Insufficient evidence for validation as a biomedical framework. Some research has attempted to correlate Dosha types with genetic polymorphisms, metabolic profiles, and gut microbiome composition, with preliminary and inconsistent results. The Tridosha framework represents a different epistemological model — it cannot be directly mapped onto modern physiology. Its value lies in its clinical and educational framework within the traditional system.
relationship: Traditional conceptual framework — no direct modern equivalent — valuable as a distinct knowledge system
safety_considerations: Using Dosha classification alone without proper Ayurvedic clinical training may lead to inappropriate self-treatment. Always consult a qualified Ayurvedic practitioner (BAMS or MD Ayurveda) for Dosha-based treatment.
sources: Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine (systematic reviews)

traditional_description: Hridroga refers to diseases of the Hridaya (heart) described in Ayurvedic classical texts. The texts describe five types of Hridroga based on Dosha predominance: Vataja, Pittaja, Kaphaja, Sannipatika (all three Doshas), and Krimija (caused by organisms). Symptoms described include chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness, fatigue, and edema — which partially correspond to modern cardiac presentations.
classical_context: Described in Charaka Samhita — Chikitsa Sthana, Chapter 26; Sushruta Samhita — Uttara Tantra; Ashtanga Hridayam — Nidana and Chikitsa Sthana.
modern_evidence_status: Partly overlapping — conceptual analogue. Some Ayurvedic herbs used in Hridroga management (e.g., Arjuna / Terminalia arjuna) have been studied for cardioprotective effects with moderate evidence. The Dosha-based classification does not correspond directly to modern cardiac disease classification.
relationship: Partly overlapping / traditional analogue — different diagnostic frameworks
safety_considerations: Cardiac conditions require prompt modern medical care. Ayurvedic approaches may complement under specialist supervision. Never stop cardiac medications based on Ayurvedic consultation alone.
sources: Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine

modern_related_concept: Preventive medicine / healthy aging / adaptogenic therapy
traditional_description: Rasayana is one of the eight specialized branches of Ayurveda (Ashtanga Ayurveda) and refers to a comprehensive system for health promotion, disease prevention, and longevity. The term means 'that which nourishes Rasa (the primary body fluid).' Rasayana therapies include herbal preparations (e.g., Chyawanprash, Brahma Rasayana), dietary practices, behavioral codes, and mental/spiritual disciplines. The goal is to achieve longevity, memory, health, youthful vigor, clarity of complexion, and excellence of voice and sense faculties.
classical_context: Charaka Samhita — Chikitsa Sthana, Chapter 1 (Rasayana Adhyaya) — an extensive chapter dedicated entirely to this subject. Also covered in Ashtanga Hridayam — Uttara Sthana.
modern_evidence_status: Some components studied. Chyawanprash (containing Amalaki and other herbs) has been studied for immunomodulatory effects — moderate evidence. Individual Rasayana herbs (Ashwagandha, Brahmi, Guduchi) have varying evidence levels for specific effects. The overall Rasayana concept corresponds most closely to modern preventive medicine and healthy aging research, though the conceptual frameworks differ substantially.
relationship: Broadly related — different frameworks — individual components have varying evidence
safety_considerations: Rasayana preparations vary widely in composition and quality. Use only from reputable, regulated manufacturers. Some preparations contain heavy metals (classical Rasa preparations) — safety profile requires expert Ayurvedic supervision.

traditional_description: Sandhivata is an Ayurvedic condition affecting the Sandhi (joints), characterized by pain, swelling, stiffness, and crepitus (crackling sound) in the joints. It is classified as a Vatavyadhi (Vata-dominant disorder). The description of pain worsening with activity and in cold weather, crepitus, and gradual onset has led to comparisons with osteoarthritis, though the diagnostic frameworks differ.
classical_context: Described in Charaka Samhita, Madhava Nidana, and Ashtanga Hridayam under Vatavyadhi.
modern_evidence_status: Partly overlapping. Several Ayurvedic treatments for Sandhivata (e.g., Shallaki / Boswellia serrata, Guggulu formulations, Nirgundi / Vitex negundo, Panchakarma procedures) have been studied in osteoarthritis — with moderate but often methodologically limited evidence. Boswellia has perhaps the strongest evidence base among Ayurvedic anti-inflammatory herbs.
relationship: Partly overlapping / traditional analogue (Sandhivata ≈ osteoarthritis conceptually)
safety_considerations: Joint pain may have various causes requiring proper diagnosis. Guggulu formulations can interact with thyroid medications and anticoagulants. Consult healthcare providers before using Ayurvedic treatments alongside prescribed joint medications.

modern_related_concept: Detoxification / therapeutic interventions (no direct modern equivalent)
traditional_description: Panchakarma is the five-fold classical Ayurvedic therapeutic purification procedure: (1) Vamana (therapeutic emesis), (2) Virechana (therapeutic purgation), (3) Basti (medicated enema — Anuvasana and Niruha), (4) Nasya (nasal administration), and (5) Raktamokshana (blood-letting, less commonly performed today). Preceded by Purvakarma (preparatory procedures including Snehana/oleation and Svedana/sudation). Used for treating chronic diseases, seasonal purification, and as a preparatory step for Rasayana therapy.
classical_context: Charaka Samhita — Siddhi Sthana; Sushruta Samhita — Chikitsa Sthana; Ashtanga Hridayam — Sutra Sthana.
modern_evidence_status: Insufficient rigorous evidence. While Panchakarma is widely practiced and reported beneficial by practitioners and patients, large, well-controlled clinical trials are lacking. Some individual procedures (e.g., Basti) have been studied with variable results. The 'detoxification' concept does not have a direct validated biomedical correlate, though some studies have explored immunological and physiological parameters.
relationship: Traditional therapeutic system — no direct modern equivalent — evidence insufficient by modern standards
safety_considerations: Panchakarma must only be performed by qualified Ayurvedic practitioners in appropriate clinical settings. Vamana (emesis induction) is contraindicated in many conditions and can be dangerous if improperly administered. Not suitable for all patients.
sources: Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine (systematic reviews)

traditional_description: Brahmi is one of the most celebrated Medhya Rasayana (brain-nourishing rejuvenating herbs) in Ayurveda. It is described as enhancing memory, intellect, and concentration while having a calming effect. Used in Ayurvedic practice for cognitive enhancement, anxiety, epilepsy, and nervous system disorders. The name Brahmi is also applied to Centella asiatica (Gotu Kola) — these are distinct plants sometimes confused in practice.
classical_context: Charaka Samhita — Chikitsa Sthana, Chapter 1 (Rasayana), classified among Medhya dravyas. Described in Ashtanga Hridayam and Bhavaprakasha Nighantu.
modern_evidence_status: Moderate evidence for cognitive effects. Multiple randomized controlled trials have demonstrated improvements in memory, learning, and cognitive processing speed in healthy adults and in age-related cognitive decline. Active constituents: bacosides. Effects are typically observed after 12 weeks of consistent use. Some evidence for anxiolytic effects. Cochrane-quality systematic reviews are emerging.
relationship: Traditional herb — moderate modern evidence for cognitive effects
safety_considerations: Generally well-tolerated. Common side effects: nausea, stomach upset (take with food). May slow heart rate — caution in bradycardia. Consult healthcare provider if taking sedatives, thyroid medications, or medications for Alzheimer's disease.
